title: Earliest known Long Count date, Chiapa de Corzo (36 BCE)
summary: A fragment of a monument at Chiapa de Corzo in southern Mexico carries the earliest known Long Count date, read as 7.16.3.2.13 and corresponding to 36 BCE. The earliest known Long Count inscriptions are generally classed as epi-Olmec rather than Maya; parts of this inscription have been lost.

uncertainty.note: The inscription is incomplete; the 36 BCE reading is a deduction from the readable glyphs. 36 BCE = astronomical -35.

as_recorded.value: probably recorded a date in 36 B.C.

where.modern_name: Chiapa de Corzo archaeological zone, Chiapas, Mexico
where.historical_name: Chiapa de Corzo (epi-Olmec setting, pre-Classic Mesoamerica)

importance.justification: Marks the earliest known use of the Long Count, the calendar system whose inscriptions run to a monument at Tonina dated to A.D. 909.

sources.title: Non-power positional number representation systems, bijective numeration, and the Mesoamerican discovery of zero
